newsitem.title: GERMANY: Santer says stability will help forge strong euro.
newsitem.headline: Santer says stability will help forge strong euro.

text.p: Strict rules to ensure stability after European currency union would help to forge a strong common currency, European Commission President Jacques Santer said on Saturday.

"I wouldn't hesitate to say that the euro has every chance of being at least as strong as the deutschemark," Santer said at a meeting of the Baden-Wuerttemberg wing of the Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democratic (CDU) party.
In December, EU leaders agreed a stability pact aimed at enforcing fiscal discipline under European monetary union.

Santer went on to say that it was vital that the criteria for EMU membership laid out in the Maastricht Treaty should be strictly adhered to. "There will not be a weak euro while I'm around," Santer said.
He dismissed calls to delay the planned 1999 EMU start date. "I am worried that if we delay the start date now, we will delay currency union for a whole generation," Santer said.
Santer said that the introduction of fiscal policies Europe-wide aimed at encouraging stability were not the reason for often high levels of unemployment.
On the contrary, he said, fiscal stability was the only way of combatting unemployment long-term.
Responding to calls by France for a "stability council" to coordinate policy among member governments after the launch of EMU, Santer said that such a body could only function on an informal basis.
A stability council could in no way be allowed to compromise the independence of the European Central Bank, he said.
The Commission head went on to say that the EU should take advantages of opportunities to expand eastwards toward eastern and central Europe.

A restructuring of the institutions of the EU was necessary. "It is completely impossible that institutional structures designed to cope with six countries can be expected to deal with 20, 25 or 30 countries," he said.
The Commission would wait until the end of the current EU intergovernmental conference to state its position on requests by 10 central and eastern European countries to enter the European bloc.
Negotiations on entry could begin six months after that, Santer said.
